title: Release Management & Versioning
summary: Version numbers and changelogs are promises to your consumers. Learn semantic versioning, release cadences, release branches, hotfixes, and the deprecation discipline that keeps breaking changes honest.

slides.markdown:
A version number is a **promise**, not a label. When a consumer sees `2.4.1 -> 2.4.2`, they should be able to trust — without reading a diff — that nothing they depend on broke.

Release management is the discipline that makes that promise reliable: choosing a versioning scheme, deciding when and how often to cut a release, handling the branch that needs an urgent fix without carrying unrelated in-progress work, and retiring old behavior without breaking everyone who depends on it overnight.

Get this wrong and consumers stop trusting your version numbers — which means they stop upgrading promptly, which is worse for everyone.

slides.subTitle: major.minor.patch
slides.markdown:
Semantic versioning (semver) gives each position in `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` a specific promise:

- **PATCH** (`2.4.1 -> 2.4.2`) — bug fixes only. Safe to upgrade blindly; behavior for correct usage doesn't change.
- **MINOR** (`2.4.1 -> 2.5.0`) — new functionality, backward-compatible. Existing code keeps working; new capabilities are additive.
- **MAJOR** (`2.4.1 -> 3.0.0`) — breaking changes. Existing code may need updates to keep working.

The value isn't the numbers themselves, it's that a consumer can set their dependency constraint (`^2.4.0`, accept any 2.x) and trust it will never silently break them, because breaking changes are contractually confined to major bumps.

A changelog written by hand at release time is slow and frequently wrong — someone has to remember every change since the last tag. **Conventional Commits** (`feat: add dark mode`, `fix: correct off-by-one in pagination`, `feat!: remove deprecated auth header`) make the commit message itself the structured input a tool can consume.

Tooling then derives, mechanically: the changelog (grouped by `feat`/`fix`/etc.), and often the **version bump itself** — any `fix:` commit implies at least a patch bump, any `feat:` implies at least minor, and a `!` or `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer implies major. This turns "what changed and how big a bump is it" from a judgment call into something derivable from the commit history.

| | Release trains | Continuous release |
|---|---|---|
| **Cadence** | Fixed (every 2 weeks, every quarter) | Whenever a change is ready |
| **What ships in a release** | Whatever landed by the cutoff | One change (or a small batch) |
| **Predictability for consumers** | High — they know when to expect updates | Lower per-release, but updates arrive continuously |
| **Blast radius per release** | Larger — many changes bundled | Small — easy to attribute a regression |
| **Good fit for** | Client-installed software, coordinated launches, compliance-gated releases | SaaS backends, internal services, anything users don't manually upgrade |

A release train exists because *someone* needs a fixed rhythm — a mobile app's App Store review cadence, a hardware/firmware release, a compliance sign-off window. Continuous release, the default for most backend services, ships each change independently the moment it's validated, which both speeds delivery and — because each release is small — makes it obvious which change caused a regression.

When main keeps moving but you need to stabilize a specific set of changes for release, cut a **release branch** (`release/2.5`) at that point. Main keeps accepting new work; the release branch only accepts fixes for bugs found during release stabilization (release-candidate testing, final QA).

This matters most for release-train models: without a release branch, stabilizing means either freezing main entirely (blocking everyone's work) or shipping whatever happens to be on main at cut time, bugs included. The branch isolates "what's going out this cycle" from "what's still cooking," and once the release ships, any fixes made on the branch merge back into main so they aren't lost on the next cut.

A **hotfix** patches an already-released version without dragging along everything that's since landed on main. The flow: branch from the *released tag* (`v2.4.1`, not main), apply the minimal fix, tag `v2.4.2`, ship it — then merge that fix back into main so it isn't lost on the next regular release.

The discipline that makes this safe is scope: a hotfix branch should contain **only** the fix, not "also cherry-pick this other thing while I'm at it." Every extra change on a hotfix branch is untested against production under time pressure, which is precisely the situation you're trying to de-risk.

**Calendar-based** ships on a fixed date regardless of what's ready — features that aren't done wait for the next cycle. **Feature-based** ships when a specific feature is complete, whenever that is.

Calendar-based gives predictability to everyone downstream — support, marketing, ops staffing — at the cost of sometimes shipping a smaller release than planned, or delaying a finished feature to the next train for coordination reasons. Feature-based optimizes for shipping value the moment it's ready, at the cost of unpredictable release timing that's harder for other teams to plan around.

Most real organizations blend the two: a calendar cadence for the *release train*, with feature flags (see the previous topic) decoupling an individual feature's actual availability from that fixed ship date.

A breaking change is unavoidable eventually — an API needs to remove a field, a library needs to drop a legacy code path. A **deprecation policy** is the contract for how that happens without ambushing consumers:

1. **Announce** the deprecation in a minor release, with the old behavior still working.
2. **Warn** — emit a deprecation warning (log line, response header, compiler warning) so consumers can find every call site before it breaks.
3. **Wait** a stated window (a common default: one minor version, or a fixed time period like 6 months).
4. **Remove** in the next major version, never inside a minor or patch.

The deprecation window is what turns a breaking change from an incident into a scheduled migration — consumers get advance notice and a grep-able warning instead of a surprise failure.

slides.sectionTitle: The numbers behind trusting a bump
slides.markdown:
Package ecosystems that rely on semver do so at real scale: a popular open-source library with millions of weekly downloads might have thousands of transitive dependents. If a patch release breaks even a small fraction of them, that's real, measurable damage across an ecosystem, not a single team's incident.

This is why disciplined semver matters more, not less, as a project gets more widely depended on: `npm`/`pip`/`cargo` dependency resolvers use semver ranges (`^2.4.0`) to decide what to auto-upgrade, and a mislabeled patch release gets pulled into production builds across the ecosystem automatically, with no human reviewing it before it lands.

slides.sectionTitle: Breaking semver as a patch bump
slides.markdown:
A team ships `2.4.1 -> 2.4.2` — labeled a patch — that changes a default timeout from 30 seconds to 5. It's a one-line diff, so it *feels* like a patch. But any consumer relying on the old default now sees new failures with no code change on their end, and their dependency manager auto-upgraded them because patch bumps are supposed to be safe.

The underlying error is judging a change's size by lines of diff instead of by **behavioral impact on consumers**. A one-line default change is a breaking change if any reasonable consumer depended on the old value — and defaults almost always have implicit dependents. That change belonged in a major version, with the deprecation flow from the previous slide, not silently in a patch.

slides.sectionTitle: Release management is a trust system
slides.markdown:
Every piece here — the version number, the changelog, the release branch, the hotfix, the deprecation window — exists to answer one question for a consumer without them reading your source: **"can I upgrade safely, and if not, what do I need to do first?"**

A team that answers that question honestly and consistently earns fast upgrades; consumers pull new versions promptly because they trust the promise. A team that gets sloppy with what counts as a patch trains its own consumers to pin versions and delay upgrading indefinitely — which is worse for security patches and bug fixes reaching them at all. [Rollback & Safe Deploys](rollback-and-safe-deploys) covers the mechanics of what happens when a release, however versioned, still needs to be undone in production.
